claim: No prior work as of the survey's analysis (through May 2024, updated through Dec 2024) demonstrates successful intrinsic self-correction (same model, in-context feedback only, no external verification) with prompted LLMs in general tasks under fair evaluation conditions.
stance_target: intrinsic self-correction fails without external verification -- the core mechanism claim underlying a target paper's degradation finding
scope_conditions: critical survey of self-correction literature published through 2024, general (non-decomposable) tasks
quoted_support: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited for self-correction

claim: Every audited claim of successful intrinsic self-correction in the literature (RCI Prompting, Reflexion, CAI Revisions, Self-Refine) relied on either oracle ground-truth information unavailable at real inference time, or artificially weakened initial-response prompting that inflates the apparent improvement from self-correction.
stance_target: prior positive self-correction results are methodological artifacts rather than genuine capability demonstrations
quoted_support: we find that many studies use either oracle information in the self-correction processes (unrealistic frameworks) or weak prompts that can be easily improved for generating initial responses (unfair settings), which over-evaluate self-correction.

claim: The bottleneck in self-correction is unreliable feedback generation, not the refinement step -- LLMs can act on good feedback when it is available but cannot reliably self-detect their own errors absent an external verifier.
stance_target: the mechanistic explanation for why self-generated feedback degrades rather than improves outputs
quoted_support: Prior studies widely agree that LLMs can refine their responses given reliable feedback. However, generating reliable feedback on their own responses is still observed to be challenging for LLMs without using additional information.

claim: Self-correction succeeds reliably only under three conditions: reliable external tool/knowledge feedback is available (e.g. code interpreters, web search), the feedback/refinement modules are fine-tuned on large-scale data (often >100K examples), or the task has a decomposable-response property making verification strictly easier than generation.
stance_target: the specific boundary conditions under which LLM self-correction/feedback can be expected to help rather than hurt
scope_conditions: cross-task synthesis, external-tool, fine-tuning, and decomposable-task self-correction literature
quoted_support: self-correction works well in tasks that can use reliable external feedback... (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction.

claim: Prior self-correction research conflates three distinct research questions (RQ1: intrinsic capability, RQ2: capability with external information, RQ3: final-output comparison against strong baselines) without clearly stating which is being tested, causing many claimed refutations or confirmations to not actually verify what they claim.
stance_target: methodological standard for what a self-correction (or by extension, iterative-feedback NAS) paper must specify to make a valid claim
quoted_support: Prior studies often simply state their research questions as whether LLMs can self-correct their mistakes... However, we claim that research questions in self-correction research should be defined in more detail.

claim: The proposed 8-item checklist for self-correction research requires (among other things) not using oracle information, using sufficiently strong prompts for initial-response generation, disclosing fine-tuning data scale, and comparing against strong baselines (self-consistency, generate-and-rank) at matched computational cost.
stance_target: concrete evaluation requirements a fair-and-realistic self-correction or feedback-in-search claim must satisfy
scope_conditions: checklist proposed for future self-correction research design
quoted_support: Comparing with strong baselines using comparable computational cost. (§6) Required

claim: Tasks with decomposable responses (e.g., verifying each fact in a multi-fact answer) are an exception where intrinsic self-correction with in-context learning alone can succeed, because verification of each sub-component is strictly easier than the original generation task.
stance_target: the boundary/rival explanation for when intrinsic self-correction can genuinely work without an external verifier, relevant to whether a CNN-architecture-generation task falls in or out of this exception category
quoted_support: Tasks with decomposable responses are one of the few groups of tasks for which verification is clearly easier than generation, which enables intrinsic self-correction. However, many real-world tasks do not satisfy this property.

claim: As of the survey's later update (through late 2024), a recent trend uses reinforcement learning (e.g., OpenAI o1) to train models to recognize and refine their own mistakes during reasoning, reported to outperform prior LLMs on reasoning benchmarks -- suggesting that where self-correction succeeds at scale, it is via RL training rather than in-context prompting.
stance_target: whether recent large-scale RL-trained reasoning models represent a genuine exception to the intrinsic-self-correction-fails consensus, relevant to model-scale dependence
scope_conditions: emerging trends noted through late 2024, OpenAI o1
quoted_support: OpenAI has published o1, a model for reasoning tasks trained with reinforcement learning to explore different strategies, recognize their own mistakes, and refine their thinking process.
